questions.stem: The MOST ABUNDANT gas in Earth's ATMOSPHERE is:
questions.explanation: EARTH's ATMOSPHERE — COMPOSITION by VOLUME (dry air): (1) NITROGEN (N₂) — 78.08% — MOST ABUNDANT. (2) OXYGEN (O₂) — 20.95%. (3) ARGON (Ar) — 0.93%. (4) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) — 0.042% (420 ppm, April 2025 — rising from 280 ppm pre-industrial; Mauna Loa record since 1958). (5) NEON (Ne) — 18 ppm. (6) HELIUM (He) — 5 ppm. (7) METHANE (CH₄) — 2 ppm + rising. (8) KRYPTON (Kr) — 1 ppm. (9) HYDROGEN (H₂) — 0.55 ppm. (10) NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O), OZONE (O₃), carbon monoxide (CO), xenon, chlorofluorocarbons — trace. PLUS WATER VAPOUR (variable, 0-4%). NITROGEN (N₂): (1) COLOURLESS, ODOURLESS, TASTELESS gas. (2) MW 28; density slightly less than air. (3) NON-REACTIVE at room temp (strong triple bond N≡N, bond energy 945 kJ/mol — hardest bond to break). (4) LIQUID NITROGEN — -196°C (77 K); cryogenic uses: food freezing, medical (cryosurgery, fertility storage), metal hardening, preserving biological samples, dermatology (wart removal). (5) NITROGEN FIXATION — crucial for life; N₂ → NH₃ / nitrates (plants can't use N₂ directly): (a) BIOLOGICAL — Rhizobium bacteria in LEGUME root nodules (peas, beans, alfalfa, clover, chickpea, lentil); Azotobacter + cyanobacteria free-living; ~200 million tonnes N/year. (b) LIGHTNING — atmospheric N + O combine into NOx, washed down as nitric acid; ~10 million tonnes/year. (c) INDUSTRIAL — HABER-BOSCH PROCESS (Fritz Haber 1909, Carl Bosch industrialised 1913, BASF Germany): N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ at 400-500°C + 200-300 atm with iron catalyst; basis of SYNTHETIC FERTILISERS — revolutionised agriculture; feeds half of world's 8 billion people; ~175 million tonnes/year. Haber Nobel Chemistry 1918; Bosch + Bergius 1931. NORMAN BORLAUG's Green Revolution depended on N-fertiliser. (6) NITROGEN CYCLE — fixation → assimilation → ammonification → nitrification → denitrification (back to N₂). (7) USES of N₂: (a) inert atmosphere in electronics manufacturing; (b) food packaging (crisps, chips — prevents oxidation); (c) fire prevention (nitrogen-filled aircraft fuel tanks); (d) refrigeration; (e) dry-cleaning; (f) making ammonia + nitric acid + fertilisers + explosives (TNT, ammonium nitrate, dynamite) + dyes + drugs. ATMOSPHERE LAYERS: (1) TROPOSPHERE (0-12 km, weather; 75% mass; temp drops with altitude). (2) STRATOSPHERE (12-50 km; ozone layer at 20-35 km; temp rises due to ozone UV absorption). (3) MESOSPHERE (50-85 km; coldest ~-90°C; meteors burn up). (4) THERMOSPHERE (85-600 km; very hot but thin; aurora; ISS orbits here 400 km). (5) EXOSPHERE (600-10,000 km). KÁRMÁN LINE (100 km) = space boundary (FAI). PAYNE-SHULTZ + KEELING CURVE (Mauna Loa CO₂ since 1958) is key climate-change evidence. 78.08%; inert diatomic; fixed biologically by legumes' Rhizobium bacteria + lightning + Haber-Bosch process.

questions.stem: Which GAS is used to FILL BALLOONS + airships, being LIGHTER than air + non-flammable?
questions.explanation: HELIUM (He) — Group 18 NOBLE GAS; atomic number 2; 2nd most abundant element in UNIVERSE (23% after H 76%) but very RARE on Earth (0.00052% of atmosphere). Named after Greek HELIOS (sun) — discovered 1868 in SOLAR spectrum (sun) during eclipse by Pierre Janssen + Norman Lockyer — FIRST element found in SPACE before on Earth. Isolated on Earth 1895 by William Ramsay (from uranium ore cleveite). PROPERTIES: (1) Lightest NOBLE gas; 2nd lightest element (after H). (2) COLOURLESS, odourless, tasteless. (3) INERT — doesn't react with anything; no compounds known at normal conditions. (4) LOW boiling point = -268.9°C (4.2 K) — LOWEST of any element; CANNOT be solidified at normal pressure (only at 2.5 MPa + 0.95 K). (5) EXCEPTIONAL thermal conductivity. (6) LOW density ~0.178 g/L (air 1.29 g/L) — makes balloons float; inert = safer than hydrogen (infamous Hindenburg 1937 fire killed 36 — used H₂). USES: (1) BALLOONS — party balloons; meteorological weather balloons; airships (NON-flammable alternative to H₂). (2) MRI MACHINES — superconducting magnets need LIQUID HELIUM cooling to near absolute zero (4.2 K) to maintain superconductivity; one MRI uses 1,700 litres liquid He; He shortages threaten MRI industry. (3) DEEP-SEA DIVING — HELIOX (helium + oxygen mix) replaces nitrogen in breathing gas for depths >30m; prevents 'nitrogen narcosis' + 'the bends'. Trimix (He + O + N) even deeper. (4) SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH — cryogenics, superconductivity, superfluidity (He-II below 2.17 K has zero viscosity — Kapitsa, Nobel 1978). (5) Welding (TIG inert atmosphere). (6) Rocket propulsion (pressurising fuel tanks; NASA/ISRO use). (7) LEAK DETECTION (small molecule escapes easily). (8) Anti-aging research (recently). (9) Nuclear reactors (coolant in HTGRs). (10) Semiconductor manufacture. SOURCES: RADIOACTIVE DECAY of URANIUM + THORIUM; alpha particles = He-4 nuclei. Trapped in natural gas reservoirs (particularly USA Texas/Kansas fields — 75% world production). Separated by fractional distillation of natural gas. FACE: HELIUM is FINITE + IRREPLACEABLE — once released to atmosphere, escapes Earth's gravity to space; cannot be recovered. World faces HELIUM SHORTAGE; critical for science + medicine. Price hikes have been frequent. India: small quantities from Kutch Rajasthan natural gas; mostly imported (US, Qatar, Algeria, Russia). Project ONGC exploring indigenous helium. VOICE CHANGE effect — inhaling helium makes voice high-pitched because sound travels faster in less dense gas (~3× air), shifting resonance frequencies of vocal tract up. Dangerous if inhaled too much — asphyxiation (no O₂). OTHER NOBLE GASES (Group 18): (1) He. (2) Neon (Ne) — signs + discharge tubes; glows RED-ORANGE. (3) Argon (Ar) — ~1% of atmosphere; filament lamps + welding. (4) Krypton (Kr) — high-brightness lamps (headlights), lasers. (5) Xenon (Xe) — car HID headlights, anesthetics, nuclear reactors as detectors. (6) Radon (Rn) — RADIOACTIVE; lurks in basements; major lung cancer risk. NOBLE GASES historically called 'INERT GASES' but xenon + krypton + radon form some compounds (XeF₂ 1962 Neil Bartlett, XeO₃, etc.) — no longer wholly inert. 2nd lightest element; NOBLE gas (inert, non-flammable); boiling point -269°C; used in MRI magnets + deep-sea diving + party balloons.

questions.stem: LAUGHING GAS used in dentistry + as a whipped-cream propellant is:
questions.explanation: NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O) — 'LAUGHING GAS'. COLOURLESS, sweet-smelling gas; dinitrogen monoxide or nitrous oxide. Discovered 1772 by Joseph PRIESTLEY. Humphry DAVY noted analgesic effects 1799 ('gas of paradise'). Used as party drug in late 1700s-1800s ('laughing parties'). PROPERTIES: stable at room temperature; less dense than air; supports combustion (auto racing cars use N₂O for boost!); non-toxic in small doses. BREAKS down at ~800°C releasing O₂. USES: (1) DENTAL + MEDICAL ANAESTHESIA — mild anaesthetic + analgesic; 'ENTONOX' (50% N₂O + 50% O₂) given during CHILDBIRTH pain relief + paramedic emergencies. NO loss of consciousness at normal doses; mild euphoria; hence 'laughing gas'. (2) FOOD — aerating propellant for WHIPPED CREAM (commercial whipped cream canisters). (3) AUTO RACING — 'NOS' injection; boosts engine oxygen supply; more combustion → more power. (4) AEROSPACE — rocket oxidiser (cheap alternative to LOX). (5) Semiconductor processing. RECREATIONAL ABUSE: 'nangs' / 'whippets' — people inhale from small whipped-cream chargers; pleasant but DANGEROUS (B12 deficiency + neuropathy with repeated use; hypoxia death); rising concern in UK banned recently; India mostly unregulated. GREENHOUSE GAS role: (a) N₂O is 3RD MOST IMPORTANT GHG after CO₂ + CH₄. (b) GWP (Global Warming Potential) = 300× CO₂ on 100-year timescale — VERY POTENT. (c) Atmospheric lifetime 114 years. (d) Atmospheric concentration rose from 270 ppb (pre-industrial) to 336 ppb (2024). (e) Sources: SYNTHETIC FERTILISERS (major — ~30% total; especially excess urea); agricultural soils (livestock manure + soil bacteria); fossil fuel combustion (esp. diesel), industrial processes (nylon, nitric acid production), biomass burning, wastewater. (f) Also an OZONE-DEPLETING substance — currently the largest ODS being emitted (replacing CFCs after Montreal Protocol phasing them out). (g) Contributes ~6% of global warming attribution. MITIGATION: reduce fertiliser use, 4R nutrient stewardship, nitrification inhibitors, precision agriculture, livestock manure management, denitrification + destruction in industries. OTHER KEY ENV GASES: (1) METHANE (CH₄) — 28-34× GWP (100-yr), 80×+ on 20-yr; ~16% of global warming; sources: cattle burps (enteric fermentation), paddy fields, fossil fuels, landfills, wetlands, permafrost. Rising fast. India is MAJOR methane source (cattle 30 CR + paddy; 3rd largest emitter). (2) CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — POISONOUS, odourless, colourless; from incomplete combustion (cars, coal, gas geysers, smoking). Binds haemoglobin 240× tighter than O₂ → tissue hypoxia. Cause of DEATH in closed rooms with faulty water heaters; carbon monoxide alarms mandatory in many countries. (3) SULPHUR DIOXIDE (SO₂) — ACID RAIN + respiratory irritant. (4) NOx (NO, NO₂) — acid rain + respiratory + ozone smog. (5) VOCs (volatile organic compounds — paints, solvents, petrol) — photochemical smog. (6) PARTICULATE MATTER (PM2.5 + PM10) — heart + lung disease + cancers. Delhi ranks among world's MOST POLLUTED capitals; 30% of GHGs from India's power sector. BHARAT STAGE VI EMISSION NORMS (2020 — BS-IV to BS-VI, leapfrogging BS-V). National Clean Air Programme (NCAP 2019) targets 40% PM reduction by 2026.

questions.stem: Which GAS is known as 'DRY ICE' in its SOLID form?
questions.explanation: DRY ICE — SOLID FORM of CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂). SUBLIMES (goes directly from SOLID to GAS without melting to liquid) at -78.5°C (-109°F) at normal atmospheric pressure. No liquid phase unless pressure raised above ~5.1 atm (triple point). NAMED 'dry' because leaves NO LIQUID residue. DENSITY: 1.5 g/cm³ (denser than ice). PRODUCTION: compress CO₂, cool + expand rapidly (Joule-Thomson cooling) → solidifies into SNOW → compressed into blocks/pellets. USES: (1) FOOD-GRADE REFRIGERATION — transport of ice cream, frozen foods, perishables, vaccines (cold chain); effective (-78°C cooling); hotter dry ice advantages (no melt, leaves no liquid, sterile; no water damage). (2) SPECIAL EFFECTS — 'FOG' or 'SMOKE' machines in theatres, concerts, Halloween events, horror films; dry ice in warm water → dense cold CO₂ fog (heavier than air, rolls downward). (3) Industrial cleaning (dry ice BLASTING — replaces sandblasting; no abrasive residue). (4) MEDICAL — transporting biological samples, organs. (5) Scientific — cooling experiments, removing wasps' nests. HAZARDS: (1) VERY COLD — frostbite on skin contact; handle with gloves. (2) SUFFOCATION — when sublimating in closed rooms, CO₂ (heavier than air) displaces oxygen; 6-8% CO₂ causes suffocation. NEVER transport dry ice in CAR with closed windows. (3) EXPLOSION — never seal dry ice in airtight container — pressure builds up from sublimation. CO₂ PROPERTIES: (1) COLOURLESS, odourless, slightly acidic taste (dissolves to form carbonic acid). (2) MW 44. Denser than air (1.52× air). (3) Not flammable; doesn't support combustion. (4) Forms CARBONIC ACID (H₂CO₃) with water; soda water/carbonated drinks. Weakly acidic, pH ~4. (5) CRITICAL point: 31°C + 73 atm; SUPERCRITICAL CO₂ used as green solvent (decaffeination of coffee, dry cleaning, extracts). USES of CO₂: (1) FIRE EXTINGUISHERS — CO₂ fires + electrical + flammable liquid fires (non-conductive; leaves no residue; suffocates flame by displacing O₂). (2) CARBONATED DRINKS — soda, cola, beer (dissolves at high pressure; fizzy when pressure released). (3) PLANT GROWTH in greenhouses — 'CO₂ fertilisation' boosts photosynthesis (1000+ ppm). (4) Welding shielding gas. (5) WATER TREATMENT — pH adjustment. (6) Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) — pumped into old oil wells. ATMOSPHERIC CO₂: 420 ppm (April 2025, NOAA Mauna Loa). Up from 280 ppm pre-industrial. Annual increase ~2-3 ppm. PRIMARY driver of GLOBAL WARMING — traps heat via greenhouse effect. Sources: FOSSIL FUEL COMBUSTION (oil, coal, gas — 90%+), cement production, deforestation, land-use change. CARBON CYCLE — CO₂ ↔ photosynthesis ↔ respiration ↔ decomposition ↔ ocean dissolution ↔ carbonate rocks. PHOTOSYNTHESIS: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Plants + oceans absorb ~55% of human CO₂ emissions (carbon sinks); ~45% remains in atmosphere. NET-ZERO emissions goal: reduce emissions + absorb rest via forests, oceans, carbon capture tech. INDIA committed to Net Zero by 2070; G20 Bali (2022) declaration aimed at 2050 global. CARBON CAPTURE + STORAGE (CCS) + Direct Air Capture (DAC) — emerging tech. Ocean acidification = CO₂ dissolving in oceans → H₂CO₃ → lower pH (8.2 → 8.1 in 150 yrs) → harms marine calcifiers (corals, oysters, plankton). SOLID CO₂ sublimes directly to gas at -78.5°C (no liquid state at atm pressure); used for cooling + fog effects + shipping perishables.

questions.stem: The VERY TOXIC gas that binds HAEMOGLOBIN 240x more strongly than OXYGEN + is produced by INCOMPLETE combustion is:
questions.explanation: CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — 'SILENT KILLER'. Colourless, odourless, tasteless, highly toxic gas. Discovered 1776 by French chemist De Lassone. PRODUCTION: INCOMPLETE COMBUSTION of carbon-containing fuels (not enough oxygen) — (1) car EXHAUST (petrol/diesel engines); (2) faulty gas GEYSERS / water heaters; (3) burning CHARCOAL in closed rooms (sigri, barbecue indoors); (4) cigarette smoke; (5) industrial fires; (6) poorly-ventilated stoves; (7) generators in enclosed spaces; (8) volcanic activity (trace). TOXICITY: (1) CO binds HAEMOGLOBIN (to form CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN, COHb) with ~240× AFFINITY vs O₂. Blocks O₂ transport. (2) Binds tightly — doesn't release for many hours. (3) Shift O₂ dissociation curve to LEFT → less O₂ delivered to tissues even if bound. (4) Effects at exposure levels (%COHb in blood): (a) 10% (heavy smoker) — mild dyspnea. (b) 20% — headache, fatigue, confusion. (c) 30% — severe headache, vomiting, chest pain. (d) 40-60% — unconsciousness, convulsions, cardiac failure. (e) >60% = LETHAL. DEATHS: accidental CO poisoning causes thousands of deaths globally each year (USA ~500/yr; India often unrecorded/attributed). Common in winter (closed windows + gas heaters) + bathrooms with gas geysers (poorly vented). SYMPTOMS: cherry-red lips (classic sign), headache, dizziness, nausea — often mistaken for flu. Chronic low exposure → brain damage. DETECTION: CO DETECTORS / ALARMS (mandatory in buildings in many countries; not in India yet). Detect CO via electrochemical or semiconductor sensors. ~5-10,000 ₹ domestic unit. TREATMENT: (1) REMOVE from source. (2) 100% OXYGEN (high-flow mask) — reduces COHb half-life from 4-6 hrs in air to ~80 min. (3) HYPERBARIC OXYGEN — 100% O₂ at 2-3 atm pressure in chamber; for severe cases; reduces COHb half-life to 20 min; also flushes CO from tissues. CHEMISTRY: CO molecule is LINEAR; C≡O triple bond (despite C's valence). WEAK partial charge. REACTIVE — can form metal carbonyls (Ni(CO)₄, Fe(CO)₅ — very toxic). USES (industrial): (1) FUEL — producer gas, water gas, syngas (CO + H₂); (2) METALLURGY — reducing agent to smelt iron ore (C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO; 3CO + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + 3CO₂ — blast furnace). (3) CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS — Monsanto process (methanol production from syngas); Fischer-Tropsch process (hydrocarbons from syngas). (4) Flame atomic absorption spectroscopy. HINDENBURG DISASTER 1937 — not CO; hydrogen airship explosion. DEADLY HISTORIC CO EVENTS: (a) 1939-45 Nazis used CO in extermination camps (Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka — diesel engines) before switching to Zyklon B (hydrogen cyanide). (b) Cardiff coal pits + mining disasters. (c) Many Indian bathroom deaths from geyser. BHOPAL GAS TRAGEDY (2-3 DEC 1984, Madhya Pradesh) — NOT CO — MIC (Methyl Isocyanate) leak from Union Carbide pesticide plant; 3,787+ deaths (official, actual 15,000-25,000 over years); 558,000+ injured; WORST industrial disaster in history. Anderson (CEO) never extradited. Settlement $470M (1989; inadequate). 2 DEC = NATIONAL POLLUTION CONTROL DAY in INDIA. 'silent killer' — odourless + colourless + tasteless; from gas geysers, car exhausts, stoves; cause of accidental deaths.

questions.stem: The GAS responsible for BLEACHING + DISINFECTION of drinking water is:
questions.explanation: CHLORINE (Cl₂) — Group 17 halogen; GREENISH-YELLOW gas with PUNGENT irritating odour. Discovered 1774 by Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele; named 1810 by Humphry Davy (Greek 'chloros' = green). DENSER than air (2.49×). HIGHLY TOXIC — lethal at 1000 ppm for 1 min; 100 ppm dangerous. USED as CHEMICAL WEAPON in WWI (first at Ypres, 22 April 1915 by Germans; Fritz Haber ironically the architect — same who synthesised ammonia to feed world). PROPERTIES: (1) Strong OXIDISER. (2) Reacts with WATER: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl (HYPOCHLOROUS acid — the actual bleaching + disinfecting agent). (3) Reacts with ALKALIS: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O (sodium hypochlorite = HOUSEHOLD BLEACH). (4) Reacts with DRY SLAKED LIME: Cl₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O (BLEACHING POWDER). (5) Reacts with METALS to form chlorides. MANUFACTURE: CHLOR-ALKALI PROCESS — electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution); products: Cl₂ + NaOH + H₂; world's largest chemical industry. USES: (1) WATER DISINFECTION — MUNICIPAL water treatment to kill bacteria + protozoa + viruses; 1-5 ppm residual chlorine maintained in pipes. JOHN SNOW's 1854 London cholera map + later chlorination transformed public health; stopped waterborne disease epidemics. Swimming POOLS chlorinated. India: CPWD + Municipal water; BIS IS 10500-2012 standards. (2) BLEACH — textiles, paper, pulp, sewage treatment. (3) PVC (POLYVINYL CHLORIDE) PLASTIC — pipes, flooring, cable insulation; chlorine industry. (4) Solvents (tetrachloroethylene = PERC, for dry cleaning — though being phased out). (5) Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) — pickling steel, food industry. (6) REFRIGERANTS historically (CFCs, HCFCs — now phased out per Montreal Protocol). (7) Pharmaceuticals, pesticides, dyes, rubber, photography. (8) WATER PURIFICATION TABLETS (chloramine). CHLORINE-BASED PRODUCTS: (a) HOUSEHOLD BLEACH (NaOCl, 5% solution) — Clorox, Vim, Harpic; disinfectant + stain remover; caution: don't mix with ammonia (produces toxic chloramine vapours + potentially chlorine gas), don't mix with vinegar (produces chlorine gas). (b) POOL CHLORINE (Ca(OCl)₂ — calcium hypochlorite, stronger). (c) TABLE SALT (NaCl; sodium chloride — not toxic as salt). (d) STOMACH ACID — HCl; essential for digestion (pH 1-2). SIDE EFFECTS + CONCERNS: (1) CHLORINATION BY-PRODUCTS — TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs), haloacetic acids (HAAs) formed when Cl reacts with organic matter in water; mildly carcinogenic; limits (WHO + BIS <80 µg/L THMs). (2) Chloramines (when chlorine + amines/ammonia react) — irritate eyes + lungs; alternative disinfectant chlorine dioxide (ClO₂, Europe). (3) OZONE (O₃) + UV — alternative water disinfection (no taste issues, but expensive; don't persist in pipes). HALOGENS — Group 17: (1) FLUORINE (F₂) — most reactive; pale yellow; even more toxic than Cl₂; tooth paste (as fluoride). (2) CHLORINE (Cl₂). (3) BROMINE (Br₂) — reddish-brown LIQUID (only liquid non-metal at rt); red-light-like flame retardants. (4) IODINE (I₂) — lustrous purple-black SOLID; antiseptic (tincture of iodine); thyroid hormone. (5) ASTATINE (At) — extremely rare, radioactive. ACID + HALOGENS cause many chem accidents. greenish-yellow toxic gas; kills pathogens in water + forms bleach NaOCl; used in paper + textile bleaching + PVC + HCl.

questions.explanation: HYDROGEN (H₂) — LIGHTEST element (atomic number 1, atomic mass 1.008; molecular mass of H₂ = 2.016); LIGHTEST gas at normal conditions (density 0.0899 g/L at STP vs air 1.29 g/L — 14.3× lighter). Most abundant element in UNIVERSE (75% by mass, 92% by atoms). Makes up stars (including Sun, where fusion creates helium). DISCOVERED 1766 by HENRY CAVENDISH; name 'hydrogen' by Antoine Lavoisier (Greek 'water-former'). ISOTOPES: (1) PROTIUM (¹H) — 99.98%, 0 neutrons, most common. (2) DEUTERIUM (²H or D) — 0.015%, 1 neutron, 'heavy hydrogen'; D₂O = 'heavy water' used as moderator in NUCLEAR REACTORS. (3) TRITIUM (³H or T) — trace, radioactive (β decay, 12.3-yr half-life), 2 neutrons; used in H-BOMBS + tritium-glow-in-dark watch dials + fusion reactors. PROPERTIES: (1) COLOURLESS, odourless, tasteless. (2) HIGHLY FLAMMABLE — burns in air with pale blue flame. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (produces WATER, no pollution). EXPLOSIVE mix 4-75% H₂ in air. (3) Boiling point -253°C (20 K); LIQUID H₂ used as ROCKET FUEL (high specific impulse; Space Shuttle, SLS, Ariane, GSLV-Mk III). (4) Low density + escapes Earth gravity + earth atmosphere has very little. (5) Forms H-BONDS giving WATER unique properties. USES: (1) AMMONIA SYNTHESIS — Haber-Bosch process (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃) — consumes ~55% of world H₂ production; foundational for fertilisers. (2) PETROLEUM REFINING — hydrogenation (crude oil into fuels + removing sulfur 'hydrodesulfurisation'); ~25%. (3) HYDROGENATION of vegetable OILS — to make VANASPATI / margarine; saturates fats. Though trans-fat concerns. (4) METHANOL (CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH) — fuel, chemical feedstock. (5) METALLURGY — reducing agent. (6) Electronics manufacture. (7) FUEL for ROCKETS — SpaceX + NASA + ISRO CE-20 + CE-7.5 cryogenic engines. (8) FUEL CELLS — chemical energy → electrical via H₂ + O₂ → H₂O electrochemistry; ZERO EMISSIONS tailpipe; used in Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo, hydrogen-powered buses, forklifts, BackUp power. Lower cost + better batteries favour EVs for cars; fuel cells for heavy transport + aviation + shipping. (9) WELDING (oxy-hydrogen torch). FUTURE — 'GREEN HYDROGEN': H₂ produced by ELECTROLYSIS of water using RENEWABLE electricity (solar, wind) — ZERO CARBON. Seen as decarbonisation pathway for industries + heavy transport + seasonal energy storage. INDIA's NATIONAL GREEN HYDROGEN MISSION (Jan 2023, ₹19,744 crore): target 5 MILLION TONNES p.a. GREEN H₂ production by 2030 + 125 GW renewables; aim to make India global H₂ hub. Reliance + Adani + NTPC + Indian Oil + GAIL + tatas major investors; GW-scale electrolyser factories being built. HYDROGEN COLOR CODES: (a) GREY H₂ — from natural gas (steam methane reforming; cheapest; ~95% current; emits CO₂). (b) BLUE H₂ — grey + CCS (carbon capture); less CO₂. (c) GREEN H₂ — electrolysis + renewables; zero carbon; pricier. (d) TURQUOISE H₂ — methane pyrolysis (solid carbon + H₂). (e) PINK H₂ — nuclear-powered electrolysis. (f) YELLOW H₂ — solar-powered. HAZARDS: HINDENBURG disaster (6 May 1937, Lakehurst NJ USA) — German airship filled with hydrogen (instead of helium US embargoed); caught fire during landing; killed 36; ended era of rigid hydrogen airships. MW 2; most abundant element in UNIVERSE (~76% by mass); highly flammable; fuel of the future — green hydrogen mission.

questions.stem: Which GAS is responsible for the ROTTEN EGG SMELL + is highly POISONOUS?
questions.explanation: HYDROGEN SULFIDE (H₂S) — distinctive ROTTEN EGG SMELL at low concentrations. COLOURLESS, FLAMMABLE, HIGHLY POISONOUS gas. MW 34; slightly denser than air (1.19×); accumulates in LOW-LYING areas (trenches, sewers, basements). SOURCES: (1) BIOLOGICAL — decaying organic matter (anaerobic bacterial reduction of sulfates); sewers, septic tanks, manure pits, swamps, stagnant waters, rotten eggs. (2) GEOLOGICAL — VOLCANOES + hot springs + natural gas wells ('sour gas'). (3) INDUSTRIAL — petroleum refining, natural gas processing, paper pulp (kraft process), rayon, leather tanning, coal mines. TOXICITY — VERY DANGEROUS: (1) At LOW conc (0.01-1 ppm) — strong rotten-egg smell. (2) 10-20 ppm — eye irritation, headache, nausea. (3) 100-200 ppm — OLFACTORY FATIGUE (paralyses smell receptors!; you can no longer smell it → FALSE sense of safety → MAJOR KILLER). (4) 500-1000 ppm — rapid unconsciousness, death in minutes (inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria — similar to cyanide). HISTORICALLY killed many sewer workers, oil refinery + drilling workers; MUMBAI sewer worker deaths (2014, 2019 — collapsed into manholes from H₂S). SEWER GAS primarily H₂S + methane. PROTECTION: (a) gas detectors (portable electronic H₂S monitors mandatory for workers); (b) forced ventilation; (c) self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA); (d) AT LEAST 2-person 'buddy system' for confined-space entry. MANUAL SCAVENGING BAN: India banned manual scavenging (PROHIBITION Act 1993 + more stringent 2013 Act); SEWER WORKER DEATHS still 100+/year due to H₂S + methane; mechanisation pushed (RobotS + machines). 'SAFAI KARAMCHARI ANDOLAN' (Bezwada Wilson, Ramon Magsaysay 2016). PROPERTIES: (1) SOLUBLE in water; forms HYDROSULPHURIC ACID (weak acid, pH ~3). (2) FLAMMABLE — burns in air to SO₂ + H₂O. (3) REDUCING agent. (4) Reacts with metals → sulfides (tarnish on silver = Ag₂S black). (5) Tarnishes copper → black CuS; 'Blacken' silverware. USES (limited due to toxicity): (1) Sulfide production for minerals + chemicals. (2) Sulfuric acid manufacture (Claus process — H₂S → S → H₂SO₄). (3) Heavy water (D₂O) production. (4) SOME DRUGS. OTHER PUNGENT / TOXIC GASES: (1) AMMONIA (NH₃) — sharp pungent smell; toilet cleaners, fertilisers; toxic at high conc (respiratory failure, chemical burns). (2) SULFUR DIOXIDE (SO₂) — irritating; acid rain + asthma trigger; volcanic + coal burning + metal smelting. (3) CHLORINE (Cl₂) — greenish-yellow, pungent; WWI weapon. (4) METHANE (CH₄) — actually ODOURLESS (natural gas smell is added mercaptan for detection). (5) PROPANE (C₃H₈) — LPG cooking gas; odourless (ethyl mercaptan added). (6) ETHYLENE (C₂H₄) — ripens fruit. (7) METHYL ISOCYANATE (MIC) — killed thousands in Bhopal 1984. (8) CYANIDE (HCN) — almond-bitter smell; inhibits cellular respiration. MONITORING in INDIA: (a) BIS Standards for industrial gases; (b) DGFASLI (Directorate General Factory Advice Service + Labour Institutes) oversees factory safety; (c) PCB monitors emissions. Safety training for workers + public is important. toxic; paralyses smell receptors at high conc (insidious); from sewers, volcanoes, oil refining, decaying organic matter.

questions.stem: The COMPONENT of NATURAL GAS (used for cooking + heating) that has the molecular formula CH₄ is:
questions.explanation: METHANE (CH₄) — simplest hydrocarbon; SATURATED alkane; TETRAHEDRAL molecule (carbon at center, 4 H at corners; sp³ hybridisation). MW 16.04; COLOURLESS + ODOURLESS (stenched with MERCAPTAN for leak detection in domestic supply); flammable. PRINCIPAL component of NATURAL GAS (70-90%); rest is ethane + propane + butane + N + CO₂ + H₂O. SOURCES: (1) FOSSIL — natural gas reservoirs (often with oil; 'associated gas') or alone ('non-associated'). Origin: organic matter buried + subjected to heat + pressure over millions of years. World reserves: ~200 trillion m³; ~45-50 years at current use. TOP producers: USA (shale gas boom since 2000s), Russia, Iran, Qatar, China, Saudi, Canada. (2) BIOGENIC — anaerobic DECOMPOSITION of organic matter by METHANOGENIC ARCHAEA (not bacteria; archaea domain). Sources: LANDFILLS, wetlands, paddy fields (~10% global anthropogenic methane), livestock (cattle belches — ENTERIC FERMENTATION; 30% global anthropogenic; 3 crore+ Indian cattle biggest emitter country), manure, sewage treatment. Cows + buffalo burp ~100-250 kg methane/year each! (3) THERMOGENIC — natural gas wells. (4) BIOGAS — from anaerobic digesters (cow dung in rural India; scaling with GOBAR-Dhan). USES: (1) COOKING / HEATING FUEL — PIPED NATURAL GAS (PNG) in homes; CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) for vehicles (India's ~5 million CNG vehicles, esp auto-rickshaws + buses in major cities post-Delhi 2002 Supreme Court order). LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas — propane + butane, NOT methane) different — used in Indian household cylinders (mostly 14.2 kg + 19 kg). (2) ELECTRICITY — combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGT); 40%+ efficiency, cleanest fossil fuel. (3) INDUSTRIAL — fertiliser manufacture (H₂ for ammonia), chemicals, steel. (4) TRANSPORT — CNG vehicles; LNG ships emerging. (5) FEEDSTOCK for methanol, acetylene, ethylene, ammonia. COMBUSTION: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + energy (890 kJ/mol). Cleaner than coal or oil (less CO₂ per unit energy; no particulates; less SO₂, NOx). METHANE as GHG: (1) 28-34× GWP of CO₂ on 100-yr; 80+× on 20-yr. (2) ATMOSPHERIC lifetime 12 years (shorter than CO₂). (3) Concentrations rising fast — 720 ppb (pre-ind) → 1910 ppb (2023) — 2.5× increase. Accelerating since 2007. (4) Human sources: 60% of total; natural gas/oil leaks, landfills, livestock, paddy fields, biomass burning, coal mines. (5) GLOBAL METHANE PLEDGE (COP-26 Glasgow 2021) — 150+ countries pledged to REDUCE methane emissions 30% by 2030 vs 2020. INDIA did NOT sign initially (cattle + paddy concerns); still considering + partial participation. Major sectoral effort needed. LIQUEFIED NATURAL GAS (LNG) — cooling methane to -162°C → liquid at 1/600 volume; transported via TANKER SHIPS. Qatar + USA + Australia top exporters. India LNG imports: Qatar, USA, UAE, Nigeria, Oman. INDIA's gas pipeline: GAIL owns ~17,000 km network. HBJ pipeline (Hazira-Bijaipur-Jagdishpur, gas from ONGC's Bombay High). CGD (City Gas Distribution) — massive rollout 2014+; ~450+ cities covered. NATURAL GAS accounts for only 6% of India's energy mix (vs global 23%); govt target 15% by 2030 (One Nation One Grid). PM-GATI SHAKTI coordinates. 70-90% of natural gas; world's LARGEST hydrocarbon reserves; pipelines + LNG tankers transport globally; 2nd most impactful GHG.

questions.stem: The IDEAL GAS LAW relates pressure, volume, temperature for an ideal gas. It is:
questions.explanation: IDEAL GAS LAW: PV = nRT. (1) P = PRESSURE (Pa, atm, etc.); (2) V = VOLUME (m³, litres); (3) n = number of MOLES; (4) R = UNIVERSAL GAS CONSTANT = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) = 1.987 cal/(mol·K); (5) T = TEMPERATURE in KELVIN. Derived by combining GAS LAWS: (1) BOYLE's LAW (Robert Boyle 1662) — at CONSTANT T + n, P ∝ 1/V (PV = constant). Squeeze bike pump → warmer gas has higher pressure. (2) CHARLES's LAW (Jacques Charles 1787) — at constant P + n, V ∝ T (V/T = constant). Hot-air balloons rise. (3) GAY-LUSSAC's LAW (1802) — at constant V + n, P ∝ T (P/T = constant). Tire pressure rises in summer. (4) AVOGADRO's LAW (Amedeo Avogadro 1811) — at constant P + T, V ∝ n. Equal volumes of gas at same T + P have same number of molecules. (5) COMBINED GAS LAW: PV/T = nR constant. STP = Standard Temperature + Pressure: (a) OLD (pre-1982, still common): 0°C (273.15 K) + 1 atm (101.325 kPa); 1 mole gas = 22.4 L. (b) NEW IUPAC: 0°C + 100 kPa; 1 mole gas = 22.7 L. NTP = Normal Temperature + Pressure: 20°C + 1 atm (not universally defined). APPLICATIONS + EXAMPLES: (1) BREATHING — lungs expand (V↑) decreasing P below atmospheric → air flows IN (inhale); diaphragm relaxes V↓, P↑ → air flows out (exhale). (2) BALLOONS — hot air rises because heated gas expands (V↑) for given P, so density drops below surrounding air. Montgolfier brothers 1783 first hot-air balloon. (3) CAR TYRES — check pressure when cold (driven tyres heat up, pressure rises). Over-inflation danger. (4) COOKING at altitude — lower atm pressure → water boils at lower temp → food undercooked; pressure cooker helps. (5) SODA bottle — CO₂ dissolved at high pressure; opening releases P → CO₂ bubbles out (Henry's Law). (6) DIVING — as depth increases, pressure increases (every 10 m = 1 atm). Divers' breath-holds shrink at depth (Boyle); rising too fast → expanding gas → embolism. (7) Aeroplane CABIN pressurised to ~0.75 atm (8000 ft equivalent) at cruise. (8) Climbing EVEREST — 0.33 atm at top; needs oxygen supplementation. DEVIATIONS from IDEAL: Real gases deviate at HIGH pressure (molecules close enough for attraction) + LOW temperature (molecules slow, attractions matter). VAN DER WAALS EQUATION corrects: (P + a(n/V)²)(V - nb) = nRT; a = attractive forces, b = molecular volume. REAL-GAS calculations use compressibility factor Z. KINETIC MOLECULAR THEORY explains gas laws: (a) Gas = large number of tiny point-like molecules in CONSTANT RANDOM MOTION. (b) Collisions perfectly ELASTIC. (c) Molecules exert no inter-molecular force (ideal). (d) Average kinetic energy ∝ TEMPERATURE (KE = 3/2 kT per molecule; or 3/2 RT per mole). (e) Pressure = collisions with container walls. DIFFUSION (Graham's Law): rate ∝ 1/√(MW); lighter gases diffuse faster. EFFUSION: escape through small hole. BROWNIAN MOTION (Einstein 1905) — random motion of pollen/particles in gas/liquid proves molecular reality. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mole — reverse-engineered from many phenomena.
